questions.question: Define scarcity and distinguish it from a shortage, explaining why wealth cannot escape scarcity.
questions.expected_answer: Scarcity is the permanent, universal condition in which resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants — it cannot be fixed because wants expand with means and refill as they are satisfied. A shortage is a temporary market situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the going price — fixed by price adjustment or new supply (the delivery van). A millionaire faces no shortages worth mentioning but still faces scarcity: wants move upmarket, and time remains scarce for everyone. Scarcity forces ranking — which want is satisfied first, which waits, which never.

questions.question: Define opportunity cost with its two exam disciplines, and illustrate it at household, business and state level.
questions.expected_answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the NEXT BEST alternative sacrificed — only the runner-up, not all alternatives. Discipline one: express it in real terms (the alternative itself), not rands. Discipline two: rank first, then name the runner-up. Household: the Saturday shift's true cost is the day of revision forgone. Business: Thabo's R6 000 machine costs the trading profit the stock would have earned. State: a billion on a stadium is a billion off clinics and schools — every budget debate is an argument about opportunity cost. Even free things cost their afternoon.

questions.question: Name the three questions every economy answers, match the three systems to who answers, and weigh the factory-and-river scenario in both columns.
questions.expected_answer: What to produce, how to produce (labour- versus capital-intensive — weighty amid high unemployment), and for whom (distribution). Market economies answer through prices; planned economies through the state; mixed economies — like South Africa — let markets answer most questions while the state corrects, redistributes and provides. The scenario: promotion column — employment, incomes, taxes funding rights; violation column — health harmed and the river polluted, an externality whose cost no price collected, threatening sustainability. Remedies: regulation, making the polluter pay the hidden cost, enforcing labour rights.
